Newborn Arctic hares emerge from the uterus at a remarkably advanced stage of development, a hallmark of their precocial life history strategy. These altricial neonates weigh approximately 105 grams [Wwb = approximately 105 grams] at birth, a value comparable to that reported for the closely related black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus). This substantial birth mass allows the young to be furred and mobile within hours of parturition, an adaptation critical for survival in the harsh Arctic environment where predation risk is high and the window for growth is short. The physiological demands of this large neonate are supported by a high maternal metabolic rate; resting metabolic measurements taken at a body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C] indicate a maximal basal oxygen consumption of 1082 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 1082 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This elevated metabolic capacity fuels the intense lactation required to sustain a rapidly growing pup through its initial days of life, during which it transitions from total dependence on milk to the onset of solid food ingestion.

Females give birth to litters ranging from 2 to 8 pups, with a recorded mean litter size of 5.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.4 pups per litter], and under optimal conditions they may produce approximately one litter annually [F_R_i = approximately one litter annually]. This moderately high potential reproductive rate is tempered by the short, intense Arctic summer, which imposes a strict seasonal constraint on breeding. The gestation period itself lasts 53 days [tg = 53 days], a duration that is maintained at the species' core body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], reflecting the rapid embryonic development possible within a warm, well-vascularized uterus. Following parturition, the lactating female must meet the extraordinary energetic demands of her litter. The weaned young, having reached a body mass of 2000 grams [Wwx = 2000 grams] by the time they attain nutritional independence, represent a considerable cumulative investment of maternal resources directed toward offspring production. This post-weaning mass, nearly twenty times the birth weight, underscores the intense growth phase characterizing the suckling juvenile stage.

Juvenile hares, once weaned, enter a rapid growth phase known as the sub-adult stage, during which they accumulate mass at a high rate while simultaneously developing the physiological capacity for thermoregulation and predator evasion. The transition to full somatic adulthood culminates in the attainment of an ultimate adult body mass of 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], a value that falls comfortably within the range of 3 to 5 kilograms reported in the Animal Diversity Web for this species. This large body size is an adaptation to the cold, as a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio minimizes heat loss. In captive settings or during field studies conducted at a controlled body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], the time since birth at which sexual maturity is reached is 300 days [tp = 300 days]. This relatively late pubertal onset, occurring almost a full year after parturition, reflects the prolonged period necessary for a young hare to achieve the skeletal and muscular development required for successful reproduction and dispersal.

The extended developmental schedule of the Arctic hare continues with the timing of weaning, which marks a crucial transition in the life cycle. Field observations and captive studies conducted at the species' typical core temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C] indicate that the time since birth at weaning is 60 days [tx = 60 days], a period that aligns closely with the 8 to 9 weeks of suckling reported in the literature. This relatively long dependency phase allows the pup to acquire sufficient body reserves and digestive capabilities to transition fully to a diet of woody plants, mosses, and forbs. Once weaned, the young hares face the formidable challenge of surviving their first Arctic winter, a period that imposes extreme selective pressure on both foraging efficiency and predator avoidance. The high growth rate sustained during the 60-day nursing period is essential for accumulating the 2000-gram mass at weaning, which provides a crucial energy buffer against the lean months ahead. After achieving this nutritional independence, the young individuals continue to mature somatically until they reach the full adult mass of 5000 grams.

Longevity data for Arctic hares in the wild are limited, but estimates derived from captive populations and field survival studies suggest a maximum lifespan recorded at 5 years, which is equivalent to 1825 days [am = 1825 days], when measured at a constant body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. This relatively modest lifespan by mammalian standards is typical of a species living under extreme environmental stress, where predation, starvation, and exposure to harsh weather contribute to high adult mortality. In comparison to other leporids of similar body size, the Arctic hare's life expectancy is somewhat shorter, a trade-off likely linked to the high energetic costs of thermoregulation and the intense seasonal boom-and-bust cycle of food availability in its tundra habitat. The lifespan of 1825 days represents the upper limit of survivorship; in practice, few individuals in the wild approach this value. The combination of a protracted period to sexual maturity and a short adult life span imposes a selective premium on early breeding success, with each female potentially contributing only a few litters over her lifetime to the next generation, each containing a mean of 5.4 pups. The overall daily reproductive output, derived from a mean litter size of 5.4 pups per litter and approximately one litter per year, translates to an annual production of about 6 pups per year, reflecting the species' relatively low reproductive rate for a lagomorph.
